---
title: "Learning from a sample"
---

Suppose we count the personal-pronoun tokens in a corpus and find that some proportion received the UD annotation `Case=Acc`. What have we learned? We have certainly learned something about the retained tokens: if there are $n$ of them and $k$ received that annotation, their annotated accusative proportion is $k/n$. But we will often want to ask a larger question. What do the sampled sentences tell us about case marking in written Turkish beyond the sentences that happened to enter the treebank? Moving from the annotation to that linguistic claim assumes that the UD label tracks the use of accusative case that we mean to study. We will make that assumption visible rather than hiding it inside the count.

That move—from the observations we have to a quantity defined over observations we might have had—is the **statistical-inference problem**. Before we try to solve it, we need to say what could have varied. We could give every qualifying token equal weight, or we could calculate one proportion within each register and then give the five registers equal weight. Those calculations answer different questions whenever registers contribute different numbers of tokens. A claim about future written Turkish also requires an account of how registers, documents, and sentences enter the population we want to describe.

So how are we going to proceed? We begin by naming the [population and sample](populations-and-samples.qmd), then study the behavior of rules that turn possible samples into estimates. With those pieces in place, we can construct [intervals](confidence-intervals.qmd) and [tests](null-hypotheses-and-test-statistics.qmd) by reasoning across repeated samples. We then turn to [Bayesian inference](posterior-distributions.qmd), which uses probability distributions to represent uncertainty about unknown parameters and updates that uncertainty with observed data. Finally, we develop numerical methods for posterior distributions that we cannot calculate by hand. Throughout, the same question will keep us honest: exactly which unobserved observations are our observed data meant to tell us about?

## What you should already know

We will rely on five ideas from the earlier notes. A [linguistic unit and its observation key](../foundations/linguistic-data.qmd#unit-and-observation-key) tell us what one row represents and which rows belong to the same unit. A [random variable](../random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables.qmd#distinguishing-the-two-spaces) describes what could be observed before we see its realized value. [Independence](../foundations/independence.qmd#why-the-characterizations-are-equivalent) is a claim about how the joint probability factors; separate rows do not guarantee it. Finally, [expectation](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd) and the [variance--covariance decomposition](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd#covariance-and-a-variance-decomposition) let us describe how a numerical rule applied to a sample behaves across possible samples. Each page links back when one of these ideas begins to do real work.

We will return to four datasets. UD Turkish BOUN gives us pronoun tokens grouped into sentences and registers. The Hillenbrand vowel data give us repeated acoustic measurements from speakers. UniMorph Turkish gives us lexeme--paradigm cells sampled from a finite resource. And, when we turn to posterior computation, 55 Provo passages give us passage-level reading-time contrasts. We will introduce the relevant rows and measurements on the page where each dataset first enters the argument; the [passage-level Student-t page](beyond-conjugacy.qmd#a-robust-location-scale-model), for instance, reconstructs the Provo contrast from the reader's first fixation onward.

## Populations, samples, and estimators

We begin by distinguishing [populations from samples](populations-and-samples.qmd). Roughly, the population names the units about which we want to say something, while the sample contains the units we observed. An [independent sampling model](independent-sampling.qmd) then turns that rough distinction into a probability model for what might have appeared in the sample.

The [pronoun case example](pronoun-case-example.qmd) makes this setup concrete with a binomial model. Once we have written the probability of the possible data, [maximum likelihood](maximum-likelihood.qmd) asks which parameter value makes the data we actually saw most probable. We then call the rule that performs this calculation on every possible sample an [estimator](properties-of-estimators.qmd); applying that rule to our realized sample gives the estimate.

Now imagine repeating the sampling process and applying the estimator each time. The resulting distribution of estimates is its **sampling distribution**. This one object lets us define the estimator's [standard error](standard-errors.qmd), [bias](estimator-bias.qmd), and [mean squared error](mean-squared-error.qmd). The same repeated-sampling framework lets us define coverage for [interval procedures](confidence-intervals.qmd) and reference distributions for [test statistics](null-hypotheses-and-test-statistics.qmd).

We will work through these ideas with one mean, paired acoustic measurements, two means from different speakers, and contingency tables. The calculations change, but the first question does not: what is the unit that could have varied independently under the model?

## Updating uncertainty with Bayes' rule

Bayesian inference begins from the same probability model for the observations and adds a probability distribution over the unknown parameters. The [posterior-distribution page](posterior-distributions.qmd) works through how [Bayes' rule](../foundations/bayes-rule.qmd) combines that prior distribution with the likelihood. The [posterior-summary page](posterior-summaries.qmd) then asks which features of the resulting distribution bear on a particular linguistic claim.

Sometimes we can recognize the posterior as a familiar distribution and calculate it algebraically. [Conjugate priors](conjugate-priors.qmd) give us one important case: after the data update the prior, the posterior remains in the same distribution family.

The remaining question is what the model says about observations we have not seen. A [prior predictive distribution](prior-predictive-distributions.qmd) answers before the present observations update the prior; a [posterior predictive distribution](predictive-distributions.qmd) answers after the update. Both bring us back to possible observable responses. Only then do we turn to [models whose posteriors cannot be normalized by hand](beyond-conjugacy.qmd), since we should know what distribution we want before choosing an algorithm that approximates it.

## Posterior computation and checking

Suppose, then, that the posterior is well defined but we cannot calculate the integral needed to normalize or summarize it. [Monte Carlo integration](monte-carlo-integration.qmd) begins with the easiest version of the problem: if we can draw from the target distribution, averages of those draws approximate expectations. [Importance sampling](importance-sampling.qmd) asks what to do when we can draw from a different distribution instead. [Markov chain Monte Carlo](markov-chain-monte-carlo.qmd) uses the [Markov-chain](markov-chains.qmd) dependence structure when direct independent draws are unavailable.

From there we move through Metropolis--Hastings, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, and Stan. Once we know what each sampler is trying to do, we can make sense of [trace plots](checking-markov-chains.qmd), [$\widehat R$](rhat.qmd), [autocorrelation](autocorrelation.qmd), [effective sample size](effective-sample-size.qmd), [divergences](divergent-transitions.qmd), and [parameter-pair plots](parameter-pair-plots.qmd). These diagnostics concern our approximation to the posterior. [Generated quantities](generated-quantities.qmd) can transform draws, evaluate pointwise log likelihoods, or simulate replicated responses. [Posterior predictive checks](posterior-predictive-checks.qmd) use the replicated responses to examine the model's implications on the response scale. A sampler can approximate the wrong model perfectly well.

The [Markov-chain pages](markov-chains.qmd) preview a symmetric accept--reject transition and link forward to the [Metropolis--Hastings derivation](metropolis-hastings.qmd#proposal-and-acceptance). The [HMC page](hamiltonian-monte-carlo.qmd) likewise previews how a mass matrix changes parameter geometry and points forward to the [full geometric explanation](mass-matrix-geometry.qmd). In both cases, the preview tells us what the device does before a later page derives why it works.

As we work, keep returning to three questions. Which population quantity are we trying to learn about? What sampling or observation model connects that quantity to the data? And what procedure turns the realized sample into the number we report? The opening token proportion, an average of register proportions, and a proportion for a broader process of written Turkish answer different versions of these questions even when they begin from the same file.

The [chapter dependency graph](../learning-path.qmd) shows how these ideas connect to the earlier probability material. Begin with [populations and samples](populations-and-samples.qmd).

## Module recap

1. Name the population, unit, target quantity, and sampling or observation model before choosing a procedure.
2. Keep an estimator or interval procedure, which varies across possible samples, separate from the numerical value produced by the observed sample.
3. Treat posterior computation as an approximation to an already specified probability model.
4. Return to the response scale and ask whether the model reproduces the features of the linguistic data that motivated it.
